summary: Detailed documentation of UCSB's Remote Job Service, following up on RFC 436. It restates the essence of the official RJE protocol in RFC 407 and describes the subset UCSB implemented, listing what was not supported. A rewrite was planned for about six months later.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 477 explains how UCSB's Remote Job Service let network users submit batch jobs to its computer and receive job status and output. The service implemented only part of the stated RJE protocol and had known limitations.

subtitle: How UCSB's Remote Job Service accepted, tracked and returned batch jobs.

tldr.problem: UCSB wanted remote users to submit and manage batch jobs on its computer through the network.
tldr.mechanism: Its Remote Job Service provides each user with a virtual HASP remote-job terminal, accepts input and output file details, and uses FTP or a direct connection to transfer files.
tldr.outcome: RFC 477 documents a subset of the official RJE protocol, lists missing commands and limitations, and says a rewrite was planned for about six months later.

facts.label: Users logged in per user name

today: The unit records RFC 477's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. This document describes UCSB's RJS implementation and its limits at the time.

sections.title: The UCSB Remote Job Service
sections.content:
UCSB's Remote Job Service (RJS) connects users to the site's HASP batch system. It gives each user a virtual remote-job-entry terminal with a card reader, card punch, line printer and operator's console. Users can manage jobs they submitted, including after logging out and back in.

The implementation supports only a subset of the official protocol. The RFC lists missing input control-card checks and job batching, only two output dispositions, no restart markers on output in FTP blocked mode, and several unimplemented commands. If an error occurs while a job is processed, RJS abandons the job and deletes any further output.
sections.plainLanguage: RJS lets a remote user submit work to UCSB's batch system and manage the resulting job. It supports only part of the protocol and may abandon a job when it encounters an error.

sections.title: Submitting and Tracking a Job
sections.content:
A user logs in with a user name and password, then supplies source and output file information and requests input retrieval. The account number is accepted as an accounting parameter, although billing is not implemented in the documented service. RJS assigns a job identifier and places the job in the user's queue for source transfer.

RJS reports when processing begins and records the job's final disposition. A user can request a status report showing the processing stage and the supplied file information. The RFC says status information is retained for at least a fixed period, then two days, and longer when storage permits.
sections.plainLanguage: The user identifies a source file and where output should go, then asks RJS to start the job. RJS assigns an identifier so the user can later check the job's progress or result.

sections.title: Two Command Styles
sections.content:
RJS offers a standard command syntax and an optional local syntax. The authors describe the standard form as suited to programs and cumbersome for people. The local form aims to feel more natural to a person using a terminal and adds commands and features beyond the standard syntax.

Commands set login and file parameters, start input retrieval, check job status, change output handling or cancel a job. RJS can transfer files through a simplex connection or FTP. File attributes specify data representation and carriage-control handling; the RFC documents the differences between those transfer methods.
sections.plainLanguage: People and programs can control RJS using two command styles. The service transfers job files either through a direct connection or with FTP, according to the requested file settings.

sections.title: Limits and Planned Changes
sections.content:
The RFC openly documents differences from the official RJE protocol and other ways the service was less than ideal. For example, the input file is not checked for RJE control cards, input files cannot batch jobs, and output restart markers are not sent in FTP blocked mode. The standard syntax also lists commands that the implementation does not support.

The author says a rewrite was scheduled for the near future, about six months later, and that many deficiencies were expected to be corrected. This document describes the existing implementation and does not report the result of that planned rewrite.
sections.plainLanguage: The documented RJS had gaps, and its author planned a rewrite to correct many of them. The RFC does not say whether that rewrite happened.
